utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Before the next witness is brought in, we would like to make an oral application to add a new exhibit to our 65 ter exhibit list. This is 65 ter 05335, and it is a memorandum addressed to the next witness, General Drewienkiewicz by the head of one of the regional centres of the KVM in Kosovo. This -- we -- it is our view that this exhibit is both relevant to the case and probative. It relates to events that were taking place on the ground immediately prior to the departure of KVM officials from Kosovo in 1999. We disclosed -- we found this witness -- this exhibit in one -- in a search of our evidence collection last week that was carried out for this witness, and it's been disclosed to the Defence, I believe that was last Wednesday, and we also have disclosed the B/C/S translation of this exhibit. The reason this exhibit was not included in our original 65 ter witness list is -- exhibit list, I'm sorry, is simply because it has only recently been located in our system. It was provided by the witness to us some years ago after he testified in the Milutinovic et al. case, and it came in a large bundle of documentation that was sent by the witness following his testimony in that case. This material was entered in whole into our evidence collection. Unfortunately, this exhibit was not located at the time, and it only recently popped up while we were doing a specific search for this witness. It is our position, Your Honours, that the addition of this exhibit will not prejudice the Defence in any way. The witness is here and will be available for cross-examination on this exhibit, and it's a document that was sent directly to him and he can speak about it. So my learned colleague from the Defence will have the opportunity to put his questions about this exhibit to him during his cross-examination. Those are my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The date of the document, Ms. Kravetz?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I didn't mention the date of the document because that is an issue. The witness has to explain; it is marked as thought to be 12 March 1999, and it contains our handwritten indication with the date, but it is something the witness himself will have to explain who made that marking on the document and why it's marked as thought to be 12 March 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you describe the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The subject matter -- it's called "Protest Against VJ and MUP," and it relates to actions taken by the VJ and MUP during the days preceding the drafting of this memorandum. And it's -- describes the situation on the ground as seen by the head of the Regional Centre 2, it -- this is a KVM regional centre, and also describes the forces that are present on the ground and that were observed operating on the ground at the time that's why we believe it's of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have copies for Your Honours in case Your Honours would like to have a look at the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will hear Mr. Djurdjic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is human to err, especially in such a voluminous case. There's another thing that worries me, though. As far as I remember - and I've read a lot about this witness - it seems to me that this correction made was made by the witness during one of the questionings, during one of the examinations, be it in Milosevic or in Milutinovic. The real problem in this document is in fact in the date on the document and the date when it was corrected. So there are two points, one thing is that this document has been known to the Prosecution for a long time and has even been used in one of the proceedings, and the only problem is about the date. But I believe the witness will clarify this. Maybe he himself wrote this, maybe not. But judging by the contents, it looks like the RC 2 addressed this to the witness. But generally speaking all that is written here has been said by the witness, so I don't think there will be any problems with the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be added to the list, Ms. Kravetz. Are we ready for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is General Drewienkiewicz, also known as General DZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems I'm late to rise on my feet at times. There's a problem with another document proffered by the Prosecution in its entirety. It's the Blue Book, 65 ter 00407. The Defence supposes the admission of this document. It's a document of over 900 pages containing reports that are sometimes sourced, sometimes not, and in all the time that this Tribunal has been dealing with Kosovo cases, it has not been translated into B/C/S. If something is to be admitted, I think it should be on a case-to-case basis, document-by-document from the book, not the book in its entirety. And I think if any parts of it are offered for admission then they should be listed in the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- we intend to tender the entirety of the Blue Book which is 65 ter 00407. I will be putting a number of questions to the witness about how this Blue Book was put together, the reliability of the information contained therein, and how different information was verified and that is contained in this Blue Book. In his prior testimony in the Milutinovic case, the witness spoke at length about this document and it was admitted in those proceedings as well; and we intend to follow the same course and apply for the entire document to be admitted. I do suggest that Your Honours defer the consideration of this matter until you've heard the evidence of the witness on this specific exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly that it has not been fully translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. The version we have currently in e-court is only in English. I believe some pages were translated in the past that were used, but we don't currently have an entire translation. The reason for that is that it's a very lengthy document and we have been unable to obtain a translation to date of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two things. Doesn't that firstly tell greatly in favour of Mr. Djurdjic's proposition that it should not be admitted? Secondly, what is the point of admitting a document if you're -- in whole, if you're going to rely on the whole when only part of it is available to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do intend to supply the Court and the Defence with a proper translation. It's unfortunately not available to date, but what -- our proposed course of action would be would be that we hear the witness regarding this document first and mark it for identification until the B/C/S translation is available. We do intend to rely on different portions of the document and it's not only those portions -- there aren't currently translations available for all the portions we intend to rely on, unfortunately, but that is simply due to the limited resources of CLSS to provide a translation to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It rings rather hollow. You're looking at the case only from your point of view, not from the Defence point of view, saying, Well, we've not quite managed to translate all that we think is useful. The book has to be studied by the Defence in whole to see what from their point of view may be useful if you're going to tender the whole book. It may be that you wish to tender only some parts of it when and if translations are available, and then it will depend upon the evidence of the witness whether the first part of the objection is sustained or not. But if you're going to tender the whole book, you've got a problem unless there is a complete translation. And the problem then is that if it's not available now what if the Defence wants to cross-examine about parts of it. The witness has been and gone. So there is some problems lying ahead, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see Your Honour's point on this matter. All I can say is we can go through some of the entries with the witness -- just due to time constraints, I'm not going to be able to go through all the entries that we intend to use from this book, but the witness is here for cross-examination of any of these portions. I understand there's a language difficulty because the current version is only in e-court. That is as much as I can say at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, as long as you identify for the Defence and for us those parts of the book you say are relevant to your case, we'll see how we progress. Well, I think we can't take it any further, Mr. Djurdjic, at the moment, but we're well alert to the issues. Perhaps we can try once again to have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Sorry we delayed you, but we got underway with one and then it turned out to be more than one procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Karol John Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand, General, that you're also known because of the complexity of your last name as General DZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a retired major-general in the British army and because the UK is unused to any name longer than three letters, it knew me as DZ which was the first and last letters of my name. It was a lot easier in the Balkans, at least they could pronounce my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Sir, I understand that in October 1998 you were seconded to work with OSCE and that you spent some time between that period in 1998 and April 1999 in Kosovo province; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was your function during your deployment in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Initially I was lent to the OSCE in Vienna by my government, the UK government, to assist with the planning of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Subsequently, in early November I was nominated as one of the deputy heads of mission, the deputy head of mission for operations; and in that role I deployed to Kosovo in mid-November, where I remained until about the 23rd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And, General, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal in relation to your -- the period you spent in Kosovo working for OSCE, this was in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you also provide a series of documents which became attachments to your statement when your statement was put together?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today have you had the opportunity to review both your statement and all the attached documentation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed this material, are you satisfied that the information contained within your statements and the attached documentation is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the 65 ter 02508 and I ask that that be received, and I also seek to tender all the attachments to this statement. I would like to point out that two of the attachments are already in evidence and these are P844 and P847. Because of the large number of attachments to this statement, what I propose to do, rather than read them out into the record, is we provide -- prepared a list of them and we would like to just provide that list to the Registry official present in court today and ask that that be dealt with via a memo and that can be filed later on in the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: These were all exhibits associated with the evidence of the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, they're all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and in the statement well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, they're all attachments. They have different 65 ter numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- in our e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statement will be received. The associated exhibits we await a list. And assuming there is no difficulty with any of them, they will be notified with their exhibit numbers at a convenient time by the Court Officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We notice the witness does not have a headset and he answers immediately after Ms. Kravetz's question. Could he be asked to take a second's pause before his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two things: The exhibit number of the statement if we could have that, and we have a problem as we're operating in several languages and there is a time delay involved and two English speakers tend to get ahead of the pace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Noted, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement will become Exhibit P996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, did you also previously testify before this Court in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have the chance to read through the transcript of your prior testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked during the course of that testimony, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think so. It is some years further on, so I might not have been able to recall quite as much detail. But on reading -- re-reading the statement, I'm satisfied that that was the best I could do at the time and I think it's -- if I try it again it would probably be the best I could do this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the transcript. This is 65 ter 05159, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now proceed to read the in-court summary for this witness. The witness is a retired major-general in the British army. From mid-October 1998 until 24th April, 1999, he was seconded to the OSCE. His role was to assist William Walker, which included setting up the administration and conducting verification on the ground in Kosovo. One of his functions was to liaise with the Serbian military. Due to the shortage of police verifiers, he also monitored the role of the MUP. He provides examples of the excessive use of force by the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo and describes meetings he had with VJ and MUP officers in this regard. He also informed FRY Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic of the excessive use of force by Serb forces in Kosovo. The witness explains that Mr. Sainovic was presented as the person responsible for Kosovo. The witness describes VJ/MUP operations in late 1998 and in 1999. He provides his observations as to the forces on the ground in Kosovo in the early months of 1999 and up to the period immediately preceding the NATO bombing, when KVM officials left Kosovo. He also speaks about serious crimes reported to the KVM by fleeing Kosovo Albanian civilians in the spring of 1999. The witness attended several meetings with civilian and military authorities during his stay in Kosovo and describes those meetings. That is the end of the in-court summary, Your Honours. I would like with Your Honour's leave for the usher to provide the witness with a copy of the documents we will be discussing in court today. Given that there are quite a number of them, I think just for ease of reference it would be easier for the witness to have a hard copy, and I have prepared a binder with that. The binder also contains a copy of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I would like to start by asking you some questions about your arrival in Kosovo in 1998, and we will start referring to your statement in this respect. At paragraph 18 you say that you travelled to Kosovo -- the capital of Kosovo, Pristina, on the 18th of October, 1998; and later on in your statement - and this is at paragraph 26 - you speak about some days later having driven from Pristina to Pec and your observations there. I just would like you, if you could summarise for the Chamber very briefly, what was the purpose of your travel to Pec and what you were able to observe during that day.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of the visit down to Kosovo was to determine what precisely was needed on the ground because the OSCE mission had been mandated without any prior planning whatsoever. And so the -- the purpose of the visit was -- the visit was led by an OSCE official, and he took with him representatives of the Contact Group, of which I was deemed to be one. And so we went down there and generally we had a series of meetings in Pristina to do with the administration of setting up a mission that would eventually be planned for 2.000 people. In the course of all this, we were very much stuck in and around the immediate vicinity of Pristina, and I felt it was important that somebody went outside Pristina to see what exactly the situation on the ground looked like, although this was not part of the formal purpose of the visit down there. So I went to the area where it had been reported that the violence had been worst in the summer, and that was the area between Pec and Prizren. And I drove down that area. In going down that area, I felt I was driving through something of a wasteland because there were very few people out and about. There was -- there were very few people working in the fields, and this is a fairly agricultural area; and I was struck by the heavy police presence at almost every intersection and the almost complete lack of people walking around in the towns and villages that I went through.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to the violence that took place in that area in the summer of 1998 as one of the reasons why you wanted to see this area. What exactly had you been told had happened there during the summer?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I relied for my information on this simply on the open-source media, but in the summer of 1998 there had been a lot of media coverage by involving reputable people going into the area and reporting back on the conflict between the Kosovo Liberation Army and the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And the impression had been gained through the media that there had been excessive force used by the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which had led to an international outcry. It had led to some of the embassies in Belgrade putting together groups of observers that went in to do more fact finding, and it led to a series of United Nations Security Council resolutions, and it led to NATO issuing an Activation Order, which meant that they were prepared to use force against -- against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia if required. So this was quite a strong -- a strong amount of reaction by the international community to what was seen on the ground in Kosovo over that summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. At paragraph 32 of your statement - and you've already spoken about this earlier - you speak about your appointment as deputy head of mission and you say you travelled to Pristina on the 23rd of November, that's when you commenced your duties. Is that -- what exactly did you carry out during your second trip or your arrival to Kosovo to take up this new position in the end of November 1998?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I had -- I went back to Vienna after the first trip and remained putting the plan together to get people and equipment together in an organised way into Kosovo. And I continued to do that until appointed to be the deputy head of mission for operations. At that point I was still running the planning, and so we appealed to other countries to provide a replacement for me. And once that replacement arrived and I had been able to brief him on what the point was in the planning that we'd got to, I then moved down to Kosovo on the date you've mentioned. From that moment, my focus was to set up an -- a series of outposts around the country as quickly as I could and as extensively as I could so that we could go out and see what was happening, and the word "verify" was an important -- an important word to us. We felt that to verify you had to be very precise on what was happening and really confirm that what was alleged to be happening really was happening. And I think it's an important word because it was not monitoring, and we've had a lot of monitoring missions in the past and I think there's a strong difference between "monitoring," which is more of a passive activity and "verification," which is an active activity. And we were there to verify, which meant we had to be more outgoing, lean out more, and to be more inquisitive.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I understand from your testimony -- from your statement that it was quite a logistical challenge to set up the mission and get it up and running?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, because the participating nations of the OSCE provided people one at a time. The first question I was asked when I said, Please can we have 2.000 people as quickly as you can let us have them. The question I got I got back was, Would you please write the 2.000 job specifications for the 2.000 posts. And so that was the ethos of the organisation that I had gone into, whereas quite often if one is asked for people, sometimes -- a country sometimes sends a group together that had been selected together and perhaps had a bit of pretraining. This was not the case. The OSCE said, Send us the positions to be filled, and we'll then send that list out to the participating nations. Those nations will have a think about it, call for volunteers, and then send their names forward. We will then have boards properly constituted that will select these people, and we'll then ask them to arrive as quickly as they can. This inevitably meant that there was a large delay being -- between being told to get on with it and people actually arriving on the ground. Some countries were very good in providing people almost unbidden, and some countries waited and waited and waited. And the result was that the situation on the ground, when we were able to begin to check what was happening, was quite different to the situation on the ground in mid-October when the -- when the original agreement was entered into. And this was a constant source of frustration to us because it was anybody's guess what had been going on in the intervening six weeks or so. I'm sorry that's a long statement, but I think it's important to invite the Court to understand that this was not an ideal situation. Not everybody involved in this process felt that it was their duty to get people on the ground as quickly as possible, and procedural -- procedural bureaucracy frustrated our wish to get people on the ground as quickly as possible and even if they had -- we had a similar amount of foot-dragging with regard to providing vehicles for 2.000 people, for providing radios and computers and even locations. All of these things had to be found at short notice by a small number of people, and it was less than perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You have mentioned or emphasized the word "verify" and said that that was your role. Could you just in brief describe what you understood to be the mandate of the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The mandate of the Kosovo Verification Mission was to report on the ground against the situation that had pertained in mid-October when there had been a series of meetings of members of the international community with members of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And from those meetings came three key documents which formed the basis of what we were supposed to confirm was happening on the ground. So verification meant confirming that the situation was the same or different; and if different, to say what in our view was the justification for this difference, what was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you understand this verification was to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We were given very little guidance. I think that probably should be amended to we were given almost no guidance. We were told to go there and get verifying, and so one of the quite wide-ranging discussions that took place with the head of mission in the course of the second half of November was, how would we verify, what would our modus operandi be, what would we seek to do, how much detail would we seek to get? And in the first instance we attempted to set out what our proposal was to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in fairly great detail and proposing that we would conduct it rather like arms control regime which they were used to doing because they were signatories to a number of such agreements. And so we proposed intrusive inspections, and we requested a great deal of detail so that armed with that detail we could confirm what was the nub of our mission, which was that the forces that had been withdrawn from Kosovo in the autumn remained withdrawn and that the forces which were legitimately inside Kosovo were the ones which were operating -- which were operating there. And to do that, it was very important to know what right looked like, what was the exact situation in mid-October when -- when we were given the mandate and -- so that we could understand what it looked like when we actually started inspecting, which was in early December, six weeks later. And we would be able to see where there was any difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before we move to the issue of the inspections you carried out, in paragraph 36 of your statement you say - and this is in the middle of the paragraph - that although it was not your role to monitor the MUP or the police, you could not help but do so, you were monitoring the VJ, and increasingly it became the case that was in your role you could not help but partially monitor the MUP. Could you explain why that was, how the situation evolved that made you monitor activities by MUP forces?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The way the mission was set up was that there would be a deputy head of mission who was responsible for operations and the operation of the VJ, the Yugoslav Army, and a separate one who was responsible for the police, for the MUP. In the event we did not receive the head of mission for police until late January and we also received very few verifiers who were ex-policemen, we therefore as December and early January wore on realised the only people on the ground who were sending reports back were what I would call the generalist verifiers, but that their reports increasingly referred to MUP alongside the VJ. So by -- whether we liked it or not, we found ourselves reporting on the actions of the MUP. As soon as we got proper, qualified police verifiers and a deputy head of mission for police, I was very relieved to hand some of that over to him. But because we were -- we did not have police verifiers, we did the best we could with what we had, and many of the people who were -- who were working for me in the early days had also worked in Bosnia and Croatia. And the MUP in Kosovo were from the same stable, I would say, with the same background, because obviously until a few years earlier they had all been part of the police forces of one country, of Yugoslavia. So they came from the same tradition; they were generally equipped in a similar way; and they often operated in ways that reminded us of the way police and paramilitary units had operated in Bosnia. My personal qualification in this was that I had previously spent 20 months in Bosnia, and as such I had dealt extensively with the police and the international community and so was familiar with many of the issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You mentioned earlier that -- you referred to three key documents which formed the basis of what you were supposed to do. I would like to turn to one of them this is P837, and it's tab 1 in your binder. And this document is entitled: Record of meeting in Belgrade, 25 October 1998. And I would ask you to turn to page 2, Roman numeral II, number 1. Are you familiar, sir, with this document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't know if that document is up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we have it. Could you comment on this document, specifically number 1 right below Roman numeral II which begins with: "Special police units deployed to Kosovo ..."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, the key here was the second sentence saying that "Combined police and special police strength in Kosovo will be reduced to their February 1998 duty level ..." It was not further defined anywhere, and our attempts to find out what that February 1998 duty level was were never rewarded with success, and so we were -- we had difficulty in confirming the base-line because we never got the base-line --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I see my learned colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The reason for that is that we have two English editions on the screen, not one in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's the same paragraph in the B/C/S that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the way the document has been provided for e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document was used previously and it's admitted, so I -- it might -- the translation may have been deleted at the time of admission, but the translation was there before it was tendered. And this was tendered, if I'm not mistaken, during the testimony of Colonel Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we have now found, I think, Albanian. It may not help Mr. Djurdjic very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just found the B/C/S version among my papers, so we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, and perhaps we'll continue our search for the right document. But in the meantime if you could continue with the evidence, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you were speaking about this document and said -- and had referred to the base-line. Can you just explain what this document is and why it is stated here that there was a need to withdraw the special forces in Kosovo to the level of February 1998.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It is my understanding that between February 1998 and the autumn of 1998 extra forces, extra MUP and VJ forces, were deployed into Kosovo and that this was considered excessive by the international community; and therefore, in the various negotiations of September and early October 1998 the agreement was reached that those forces which had been brought in from outside Kosovo would leave Kosovo and that the strength levels and units involved inside Kosovo would revert to this level, the level of February 1998, i.e., the level before the current crisis began.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to turn the page, look at numbers 2 and 4 which refer to additional heavy weapons and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S number 2 I believe it's on the same page, and so is number 4. But in the English it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if you could first comment on number 2 which refers to additional heavy weapons or equipment brought into Kosovo from the VJ to police or special police will be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I think this -- we took this at face value, that heavy weapons had been brought in. The significance of that is that heavy weapons were seen by the international community as being something which had been used in order to use disproportionate force, and from our point of view heavy weapons were things that were fairly relatively easy to spot. And therefore, if we knew what was there originally, we would - provided we had the right level of identification of it - be able to see whether or not anything extra was there. Specifically, every one of these heavy weapons has a serial number and because of that we sought the serial numbers of all heavy weapons authorised to be in Kosovo, and then it would be relatively easy to check against such a base-line when we came across a heavy weapon to say, Is this a legal heavy weapon which is allowed to be here or is it one that's not allowed to be here. If you don't have those serial numbers then one tank, one anti-aircraft gun looks very like another. So that was to our mind the importance and the significance of that paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I would ask you to move to paragraph 5 which refers to all VJ elements remaining in Kosovo were to return to garrison except for three company-sized teams in -- which are to remain in their localities that are referred to there. Could you comment on that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, this was one of the few very concrete facts that was verifiable inside Kosovo about the positions of the VJ; and according to this, the only places that the VJ were authorised to be was in their barracks or at these three locations which were said to be manned by company-sized teams. And we had a fair idea of what a company-sized team looked like, it would look like up to 150 soldiers with maybe 10 to 15 armoured vehicles. So we felt that this was a very helpful part of this statement, and it was one that we were able to verify, and because of that we kept particular tabs on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now I would ask you to look at paragraph 8, which refers to the obligation of both VJ MUP commanders to provide the KDOM OSCE with detailed weekly reports on a number of issues and also immediate notification on any deployments contrary to these provisions. Based on your experience on the ground, could you comment on the implementation of this provision, paragraph 8, yes.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, this was very poorly carried out. We did not receive detailed, weekly reports at all. We -- on any of those matters. We occasionally were told verbally that something was intended to happen, not on a regular basis but on a rather ad hoc basis normally very close to the thing happening, often a telephone call that gave rather sparse details. And so this was never provided to my satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you could turn the page, this is the last page, Roman numeral III. I'm interested in your comments on the sentence starting with: "However, as a last resort and consistent with the right of self-defense, the state authorities retain the right to respond adequately and proportionately ..." Could you comment on that and how you saw that part of this document implemented.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think there was any concern over this on our part because, frankly, we would have been surprised if this had -- something like this had not been -- the Yugoslav authorities were the legitimate sovereign state in Kosovo, and so of course they had the right to respond adequately and proportionately, as it reads. Our problem was that it was very rarely proportionate, and when it was disproportionate, we had a problem. And that is really the story of the KVM, responding at short notice to disproportionate violence and actions by the state authorities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say "this is the story of the KVM, responding at short notice to disproportionate violence," could you provide more detail as to how you would respond and what you mean by "disproportionate violence"?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I mean using heavy artillery and tanks and machine-guns against -- against aggravation which when you used those sort of forces it was very inaccurate and it was unlikely to hit the intended target. It was much more likely to produce casualties who were by-standers who were not involved and there were better ways of doing it. It is not the way you deal with an insurgent population, in my view. And in all of the military education that I've taken part in, it has been made quite clear that you do not shell a village simply because a couple of rounds have come out of the village. This sort of activity was observed by us on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when KVM verifiers observed this kind of activity what kind of action did you take? You referred to responding at short notice to this type of violence. What sort of response would you carry out?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, we had very limited sanctions. I mean, we would -- if we had someone on the location, then they would report what they saw. They would attempt to make contact with the commanders on the ground while we, in Pristina, attempted to make contact with our counterparts, the senior liaison people, and ask what was happening and ask why it was necessary and usually why that we had received no notification of this and would attempt to talk the situation down. We would do it by -- if the KLA were involved, we would do it by trying to get people onto their side as well and for -- to get them to respond in a less violent way as well. So we were talking to both sides, but this agreement refer -- is an agreement specifically between the international community and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And so as far as this was concerned, there was an obligation on their behalf to let us know if they were going to do something that involved moving forces out of barracks or away from the three company locations that were described earlier in the document. And this very rarely happened, and when it did happen it was about -- well, it was at short notice and was not sufficiently specific or timely to allow any discussion. It was a statement that we're going to do it and we're getting on with it rather than we're proposing to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to making attempts to contact senior liaison people in Pristina when you were -- observed this type of actions being carried out. During your meetings with either MUP or VJ representatives, did you ever raise the issue that you considered that this type of response was not considered in compliance to the agreement that we just saw or was not authorised? Was that issue ever raised?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, the word I used many, many times was "disproportionate," and I think the word "disproportionate" probably featured in just about every meeting I had with General Loncar and the other -- the other liaison people. So we were quite clear that this was disproportionate, that it was alienating them still farther with the local Albanian community and we saw it as counterproductive and leading to escalation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that the word you used was "disproportionate." Did you actually explain to General Loncar or the other liaison officials that you met was -- what you meant by this?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, many, many times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how was this explained?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I explained that if you are -- that disproportionate force simply alienates everybody in the population. It causes casualties who are not necessarily the guilty party that they're looking for, and that therefore it is counterproductive, and that they would do much better to employ less force, to arrest people rather than shooting at them, and to then get evidence and put them on trial. And if they did that, then that was, in my view, the appropriate way for a sovereign state to deal with disaffected people, with people who were behaving criminally, who were using fire-arms, who were abducting people. It was not that the activities of the KLA were not reprehensible, it was that the way that the sovereign state sought to deal with the KLA was in itself reprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you to move to tab 2 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, Your Honours, Exhibit P836, if we could have that up on screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a document entitled: Understanding Between KDOM and the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia." Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Shaun's-Djordjevic document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Let me just check that that is up on the screen. I would like for you to look first at paragraph 1 of this document which refers to "All check-points will be dismantled ..." and it sets the obligation of establishing 27 observation points on the lines of communication and one-third of these observation points will be manned initially. Can you please comment on that paragraph, whether this was complied with.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, I'm trying to gather my thoughts. We did not immediately look at this because this was -- was police business, and so we started with the VJ as -- because they went round in bigger numbers with heavier equipment and were, frankly, easier to monitor. And so when we began looking at things in December, when we had 300 people inside Kosovo, we concentrated on the easier tasks. As our numbers increased and as the overall level of violence began to increase and as we realised that we aren't going to be getting lots of policemen arriving in short order, we came to the conclusion that we would have to look at this. And so the first comprehensive attempt to look at this was made in early January when in on a single day we sent everybody we had out to check on these -- on these observation posts and to check whether or not they were manned. And when we came back and counted them all up, we found that the majority of the 27 were manned rather than one-third. One-third was obviously nine. More than -- the majority was more than -- 14 or more, and therefore this was, to our mind and as we reported it, non-compliance. So when we made the first comprehensive check of all 27 on the same day, we discovered that more were being manned than was allowed for in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when you made that discovery, that more observation points were being manned than what was allowed for in the Shaun Byrnes-Djordjevic agreement, did you address this issue with MUP officials in Pristina; and if yes, with whom was this addressed?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was certainly addressed and it would have been addressed at the -- in two ways: One in the meetings with General Loncar that I had, but separately in the meetings between the MUP liaison officer and his MUP counterpart. So I'm confident that this was reported to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say "the MUP counterpart," whom exactly -- if you recall whom exactly that would have been raised with, this issue?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think it was Colonel Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at this document, paragraph 3 refers to the withdrawal of -- of the police will withdraw stationary forces, and there are a number of localities mentioned there. Earlier you had spoken about a base-line and the need to have a base-line to be able to conduct your verifications. Were you given base-line figures and information regarding police forces on the ground in order to see whether this paragraph was being implemented or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, we weren't, and even if we had been it would have been very difficult because the nature of a police force is that in order to provide 24-hour cover seven days a week and every day of the year, everybody isn't on duty at the same moment. People are off duty, on leave, on detached duty; and so it would have been extremely difficult to take a roll-call of all of the police on a particular day. When a policeman is not on duty, he's normally in civilian clothes, so how would we have been able to do that? It was particularly difficult, and it was made -- rendered impossible by not having a base-line.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what about for the VJ, were you provided base-line figures as to the strength of the forces of the ground when the mission was set up and you started your verifications?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. This was information that we requested in Belgrade and initially via a letter from Ambassador Walker to Milosevic and followed up by a meeting that I had in Belgrade at the end of November, and the specifics that were asked for were the details of the units, their strengths, their heavy equipment, down to the serial numbers of the weapons. And that was not provided. We were provided with, at my suggestion I have to say, details of the overall figures of heavy weapons and the units that they belonged to and the locations at which they were. But that was global figures of the number of, say, T-55 tanks and the location and the subordination of the unit. And it did not go into any detail as to the serial numbers or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see from this document that it was an understanding between the KDOM and the MUP ministry, and based on your statement I understand that the KDOM preceded the existence of the KVM. Was the KDOM provided with any base-line figures, either by the VJ or the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I am -- I have been told that they were in the period since 2002, but this was never made clear to me in the -- on the ground in 1998 and 1999. I certainly never received any detailed figures from them, and in doing this, our task was made quite difficult by a very high level of turnover of the individuals in the various KDOMs so that there was very, very little collective memory inside the KDOMs. Shaun Byrnes himself was not to be found in Kosovo for weeks on end; he was based outside the country. And so it was very difficult to track him down as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you were told in the period since 2002. From whom did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think I was told it in the course of my appearance here in 2002 by, I think, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. But you -- although these figures may have been provided to the KDOM, did you request them nevertheless from Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, at every stage. When we said we've got to have the base-line figures, the response was, Well, we've already provided them. So we said, Okay, to whom? Tell us who you gave it to, when; and we were never given a satisfactory answer. So my response to that was, What is the harm, given that we are here to verify things, so that we can say whether things are going well or badly, what is the harm of giving us an extra set of this document or documents whatever they are? That way we can tell you that you are in the right or in the wrong. And this was never done. This was brushed off at every -- at every time that we made this request. It would have been the work of five minutes to run whatever the document was through the photocopier and hand it to me, and nobody ever bothered to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you to turn to tab 3 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is for reference P838.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we'll wait for that document to come up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't believe that's the correct document. This is P838.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Oh, yes. If we could have page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this document; and if yes, could you explain what it is?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that was drafted partly by me as a result of the deliberations that took place inside the mission as to how we were going to verify, how were we going to carry out our -- the task that we had been given. And the intention of the document was to make a set of proposals which could have been the basis for discussion. We did not necessarily expect this document to be accepted as written, but we did expect there to be discussion about it. And we were ready to have that discussion. We had -- we had someone with us who was an arms control inspection expert who had helped us draft this, and we felt that given the -- the references to various sorts of weapons that had been contained in the three key documents that set up the KVM or the referred to -- activated on the ground in Kosovo, that this was a way that we would be able to carry out the verification that stemmed from those documents. And so, remembering, for instance, that the Djordjevic-Byrnes document referred to check-points and observation points, it was important to agree what constituted a check-point, what constituted an observation point. Heavy weapons, again, if you go to three different arms control specialists, they will give you three different versions of heavy weapons. In some agreements heavy weapons are anything with a gun less than 75 millimetres. That's a quite big gun. And so knowing that 12.7-millimetres calibre was mentioned, we used a definition that was appropriate to that. Again, we'd heard about -- we'd been -- learned about three company-sized teams. So we said, Okay, to make it easy for everybody, let's agree what a company-sized team is. So this is really an attempt to set out -- again, what right looks like, and it was sent and we were never engaged on the detail of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that this is a letter to President Milosevic, and it's sent or -- by William Walker. Earlier in your evidence when I asked you about requests for base-lines you spoke about a letter sent to from Walker to Milosevic. Is this the document that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see here on the third paragraph that it says, paragraph starting by: "OSCE requires detailed information on all FRY/Serbian security forces in Kosovo." Did the mission receive any sort of response regarding this letter, specifically that request?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There was no response to that specific request. The response to the letter was a -- I think a phone call from Sainovic to Walker, saying that it was most improper that he should write direct to the president and he should not do it again. And I think that was the substance of the phone call. The question of whether or not it was possible for this letter to be passed from Milosevic to the appropriate authorities possibly with the words "please fix" written on it in Milosevic's hand seems not to have occurred to him. But obviously that's what we were hoping that who -- that because we didn't know the exact subordination of everybody inside the Government of the Republic of Yugoslavia, we were not convinced that by writing to anybody else we would get the right response. We might well get the response, Well, you've written to the wrong person and you should have written to the Ministry of Economics, as well as the Ministry of the Interior, as well as the Ministry of Education, or whatever it was. And, therefore, we wrote it to the top since he was in charge and he was perfectly capable of sending it to whichever the departments of his governments were that were involved in this. That was the purpose of sending it to the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 63 of your statement you indicate that you intended to meet with General Perisic at the end of November 1998, but instead on the 27th of November you met with his replacement, General Dragoljub Ojdanic. Can you just briefly explain what was the purpose of this meeting and what was discussed.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The purpose of the meeting was to follow-up on this letter, and so this was the next stage. And we expected that by this stage the letter from Walker to Milosevic would have filtered down and that therefore the Chief of the General Staff would have been in a position to have a meeting at which we began to go into detail. We had the meeting. We thought we were making a bit of progress, and -- well, I'll stop there. We had the meeting, and we thought we made some progress.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And whenever you met with different officials, was the general practice of -- for you to have notes taken for you about these -- the different meetings that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I normally had a notebook with me on -- in which I either had glued some speaking notes, some check-points, a list to make sure that I covered the thing -- I mean, before we went into a meeting, I would sit down with my people and we'd go through what was the desired outcome of the meeting and how we thought the meeting might be conducted, what we'd thought we'd get out of it. And so, in order to help me on that, I would often have that -- a series of bullet points on a piece of paper that was inside my book, and then I'd write on it as I went through the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to turn to tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And for reference this is 65 ter 02535, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, this is a page photocopied from one of my books.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you explain what it is.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It is a record of the meeting in -- no, it's a series of notes for the meeting after the Belgrade meeting with General Ojdanic, and this would have been put together by one of the note-takers with me and given to me before the next meeting. The next meeting was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before you --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before you move to that, I would like to concentrate on this document. We see under the heading "FRY information baseline," that it says: "In order to conduct verification ... we need to begin with a complete and detailed baseline - provided by the FRY." And later on, this is the fifth bullet point it's -- the document says: "We are also waiting to receive information concerning the police and special police forces ..." Can you comment on those two aspects of the document.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This document says we are still waiting, and indeed we are still waiting, now, today. We never received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The document on page 2 under the heading "Troop Rotation" indicates that at the meeting with General Ojdanic he mentioned the scheduled early December rotation of Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you indicate what sort of information you received on this specific aspect.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: In the meeting in Belgrade, General Ojdanic said, Look, we are about to drive out of Kosovo a number of conscripts who are at the end of their tour of duty, and we're about to replace them with an equal number of conscripts who are coming in to Kosovo to begin their tour of duty. And we don't want this to be misconstrued as reinforcement. And I said, Right, well let's, you know -- let's help you here. Let's agree to verify this, and then we can -- we can send the report back up the line to say that this has happened and it has happened correctly and we're satisfied that this does not constitute reinforcement. So the meeting in Belgrade gave us this as something concrete at a time when concrete information was very hard to come by. And so we said, Let's concentrate on this, let's propose a way of ensuring that this is seen to be legitimate and not breaking any agreements. We were particularly keen to do this because it was -- it was perfectly possible for other sections of the international community to see this possibly through aerial observation and not necessarily to be aware of the circumstances that only someone on the ground would see. And so what I didn't want was NATO suddenly running an air observation mission and seeing truck-loads of military trucks full of people going into Kosovo and drawing the wrong conclusions. So it was in everybody's interest that this was done properly. Now, it having been proposed by General Ojdanic, it was then discussed down in Pristina and nothing came of it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence it's 02535.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P998, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, could you now turn to the next tab, this is tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 02536.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Again, this is a page photocopied from my books -- the same book, possibly the same -- it's within a page, I would say, of this. It's the same period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see it's entitled "talking points for Belgrade meeting (27 November 1998)." Would this be a reference to the same meeting that you've been speaking about now?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, the paper that I just looked at would have been the result of this meeting, and this is the talking points for the Belgrade meeting that would have been prepared before the meeting and which I would have gone through with all of my helpers before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit and ask that it be received it's 02536.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P999, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we have just a couple of minutes before the break, if we could very briefly turn to tab 6 and this is 65 ter 02543, and I believe in your binder you have both the signed B/C/S copy and the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We're waiting for the document to come up. If you could tell me if you recognise this document and just explain it briefly, and I'm specifically interested in paragraph 3 of the document.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was the letter that I drafted when we got back to Pristina, to the Chief of the General Staff. It was an attempt to confirm what had been agreed at the meeting and to look -- to remind him of what I believed had been agreed at the meeting. And so paragraph 3 describes what I intended to do next, and again I was very keen that I was not surprising people at this stage. I felt it was important that we were transparent in our dealings, and so that we would announce an intention and then carry out that intention after sufficient time had been -- had elapsed for the people who had been forewarned to take action, take appropriate action down their chains of command. And so my point here is I will next make contact with the commander of the Pristina Corps. I was hoping that as a result of that or as a result of the meeting the previous day, a couple of days earlier, that a message would go down to the commander of the Pristina Corps saying, You have to meet with the chap, DZ, and then General Ojdanic would, no doubt, have told him how cooperative or uncooperative he was to be. And so it was simply working down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's time for the break. I wanted to conclude with this document, but I just have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does the document have a date?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was just going to ask the general that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The original in the local language says Pristina, the 2nd of December, so I've got no reason to believe that that is not the case. Where I am in difficulty is whether or not this was actually sent. I certainly signed it, as you can see, but at almost exactly this time a message came from General Loncar saying that the meeting was off. So this -- this -- either this letter was sent and no response was ever received to it, or the letter was literally about to be sent and we received the message from General Loncar that there was to be no meeting with the commander of the Pristina Corps. All liaison was to go through him. But I believe that this -- irrespective of that, this accurately reflects where I thought I was on the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender that before having the break, this is 65 ter 02543.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1000, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it's now time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must now have the break. We resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My apologies for the delay. I was delayed with another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before moving on to another matter, General, right before the break we were speaking about your meeting with General Ojdanic and you had indicated before we were looking at this documents that you had felt when you left the meeting that progress had been made and you stopped and didn't elaborate on your answer. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I went into the meeting in Belgrade with the Chief of the General Staff and his people with fairly low expectations. I did not expect him to say, We will do everything that is laid down in the letter from Walker to Milosevic. I did expect there to be the beginnings of a debate. And we began to get -- I thought we began to get that. I made the proposal at that meeting that we should begin with the information which was already in the hands of the OSCE, namely, the arms control data, which, of course, I already had anyway. But I wanted the Chief of the General Staff to agree that that was a good place to start, while there was debate among the Yugoslav side about how much further to give. And he said, Yes, okay, we'll do that. And so that was slightly positive. The other positive thing was the proposal by the Chief of the General Staff that there should be some action taken to ensure that there were no misunderstandings about the rotation of conscripts. Now, this was something we hadn't thought of, and therefore we responded to it positively and said, Yes, that's a very good idea. Let's work together to try to see how we can achieve that. So having had that meeting and having agreed at the meeting that the next step was for me to go to the commander of the Pristina Corps and go down into a greater level of detail, and while we were setting up that meeting that there -- there would be continued consideration on the Yugoslav side of the detail to which they were prepared to go, that was not negative. It was not totally positive, but I was -- I was looking for the positive at that stage and there was enough positive in the meeting for me to feel that we had a basis for future cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was the issue of training to be conducted by VJ troops also raised at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I don't think it was, but I would need to look at my notes that are here if -- and I could possibly help you some more there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I may refer to your statement, at paragraph 64 you indicate that you were informed that Serbian officials were intending to undertake normal military training within Kosovo outside barracks. Was this an issue raised at the same meeting or were you informed of this at a later stage, this paragraph 64?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I honestly cannot remember. It may have -- it may have been mentioned in the margins of the meeting in Belgrade or it may have been -- it may have been in a subsequent meeting in Pristina. But the issue was raised that there was intention on the Serbian side to conduct out-of-barracks training; and my response, wherever it was, wherever that proposal was made or that suggestion was made was provided -- it was properly documented, provided we were aware of it, then it was something we could verify, that it was the proper training. So I did not immediately believe that that was out with the terms of the various agreements. It seemed a necessary part of having a conscript army to me, provided it was -- provided it was done properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did this happen, that you were notified of the intention to conduct training out of barracks whenever such training was carried out?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, we were notified when we were back in Pristina that it was intended that there should be some out-of-barracks training. This came up at a meeting with General Loncar when he said that as part of the training of the conscripts they needed to be trained in tank driving, and it would be carried out on what he described as their local training area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where was that, the local training area where this tank driving was supposed to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I asked for details of it because I expected that it would be something which in -- in Yugoslavia would have been described as a polygon, namely, an area of land owned by the military where military would carry out such training, and such areas do exist elsewhere in former Yugoslavia. So I wanted details of where this place was, and we were eventually given details of a very small area that was said to be military land only a few hundred metres by a few hundred metres, but that the area to be exercised over was not military training land but normal agricultural land, which I was surprised by. But I was told that this was where it had always been carried out since time immemorial.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We will return to the issue of training a little bit later, I just would like for you to turn tab 7 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 02545. If we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a letter dated 12th December 1998 from Ambassador Walker to Mr. Nikola Sainovic. If you could take a moment to have a look at that. Could you tell us if you're familiar with this document, and in particular if you could comment on paragraph 2 of the document which refers to daily meetings with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that I had a hand in drafting for the head of mission. It -- it was a follow-up to a meeting that had taken place with Sainovic in -- in Pristina a couple of evenings earlier, and which -- a meeting which had been quite stormy and had produced no -- no positive outcome. And we had agreed that the right thing to do was to place on record once more our formal concern that we were not getting the information that we needed. And in the course of the meeting with Sainovic two evenings earlier, the outcome had been for Sainovic to say, Well, you need to give me details of what it is you really want. You can't just expect me to know this instinctively. And so this was the response. And so paragraph 2 was the situation as we understood it, namely, that every day there was a meeting with the MUP liaison officer and at that meeting a shopping list of what had happened in the previous day was discussed. And as you can see, we said what the information was that we were getting and we regarded the notification on police rotations as scanty with no detail on manpower and weapons. And in this respect it has to be remembered that the police in this area at the time did not -- did not go on patrol rather like the police here or in England; they had access to considerable numbers of heavier equipment. And it was my personal experience in Bosnia that we had examined the contents of various police stations and had discovered armoured personnel carriers, rocket-launchers, and heavy machine-guns, and mines, and explosives, which were not generally regarded as instruments of policing. So we wanted to know what exactly they were equipped with and where it was, and we were not getting the answers. So that's the background to that second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to a meeting with Mr. Sainovic. Who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The principal -- the principals at the meeting were Walker and Sainovic. In attendance was General Loncar and myself, and I'm pretty sure that Ambassador Gabriel Keller, the deputy head of the KVM was also present. Those are the ones I can remember with assorted note-takers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on the information that you had at the time and your interactions with Mr. Sainovic, what did you understand his role in Kosovo to be?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: His role appeared to be the person -- that of the person in Belgrade directly responsible for all affairs in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you understand him at the time to have any sort of authority over the forces deployed on the ground, either MUP or VJ?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. He appeared to be in the chain of command of all of the forces on the ground. We discovered that later when, in some of our dealings in January, Ambassador Keller spoke on several occasions to Sainovic and gained the firm impression that Sainovic was in a position to say yes or no in regard to incidents that were moving quite fast. So he wasn't several degrees detached, needing to be briefed at every moment; he was aware of what was going on on certainly an hour-by-hour basis, if not a minute-by-minute basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And based on the information you got, did any of the persons that you interact with, be it the MUP liaison officers or VJ liaison officers, did any of these persons report to Mr. Sainovic on developments on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware that General Loncar certainly interacted with him directly and I became aware of that increasingly as time went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. This is 65 ter 02545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1001, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to pick up from your last answer. You said that you were aware that General Loncar interacted with him directly and you became aware of that increasingly as time went on. Could you elaborate on your answer exactly what sort of information you had between the interactions between General Loncar and Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There would be moments when he would say I need to talk to him, would go out for five minutes and come back and say I've talked to him. So he had presumably spoken to him on the phone. On other occasions, he would come in and say, I have spoken with Sainovic already and the answer is whatever the answer was. So he was used -- he appeared to be -- General Loncar presented himself as someone who was answering direct to Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just, if you can, remind us who General Loncar was.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: General Loncar was the retired officer who was nominated as the principal military liaison to the mission. He was not the only senior liaison, but he was the one with whom I dealt with most frequently over the issues of VJ and MUP activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now turn to the next tab, this is tab 8?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 02540, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
