utterances.text: I see the document is up. Do you recognise this document, General; and if yes, could you comment? I'm specifically interested in the first bullet point which refers to the MUP agreeing to provide full details.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is a note provided by one of my liaison officers to the head of mission and the deputy head of mission, Walker and Keller, who wanted regular updates on how we were getting on with verification. And this was required because this was not the only thing we were doing. We also had a responsibility to prepare for assisting with elections, and we had a responsibility to deal with the civilian authorities as well as the VJ and MUP. And all of these activities were all going on in parallel, at the same time. And so there was a tendency on different days to ask to be briefed to be brought up-to-date on specific subjects. It was also the case that Keller and Walker spent -- spent time up in Belgrade and up in Vienna, and therefore would not necessarily be sitting fully aware of everything that was going on. And so there was a need periodically to bring them up-to-date, and this is a -- really, a statement of where we were on the 16th of December for the benefit of the head of mission and the deputy head in my presence. So this is really a summary of where we thought we were on the 16th of December, looking back on all the various meetings that had taken place up until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was this information that's referred to in this memo actually provided? It says full details regarding police movement, including times, numbers, and locations.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, it never was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we look at a bullet point that's right in the middle of the document it says: "It is stated in both meetings that the MUP and the VJ did not conduct joint patrols." Why did this issue come up of joint patrols by VJ and MUP, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is because in the summer there had been a lot of speculation, and when I was preparing in Vienna there was speculation about who was in charge of these operations in the field, where MUP and VJ were both present. And it is normal that one of the parties is in charge. And it's a very significant indicator of how a campaign or a set of circumstances is going, the point at which the -- you go from the police being in charge and the army being in support to a different situation. So we were very keen to know what the command and control situation was, and we had gone down there convinced that there were separate chains of command for the MUP and the VJ which is really what you would expect. And we were seeing evidence on the ground that the VJ and the MUP were patrolling together; in other words, there were VJ and MUP at the same location at the same time, appearing to be aware of the presence of one another. And so we said, Are you conducting joint patrols? And you can see the answer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 02540, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1002, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I will ask you now to turn to the next tab, tab 9 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 02546, and if we could have that up in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I would again ask you if you can explain what this document is, and I'm particularly interested in the first paragraph of the document which starts with: "We have noted a number of instances ..."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think this is the report to -- it is part of a report to me by -- by, again, one of my liaison officers which was part of the preparatory work for the note we've just looked at. And so this is the report to me where VJ and MUP appear to be in a joint location or working closely together, which is in our view unusual. So it is actually confirming what I described a moment ago, and that's the -- that's the evidence. Now, VJ tanks and MUP at the VJ position was a specific time, a specific place. VJ seen entering the police station in Pec today," again you know, why would the army go into a police station? They would go into the police station for a meeting, a meeting to, no doubt, discuss the current situation. It could have had an entirely innocent context, but it was worthy of note. And I don't know how many VJ, but I suspect that the very fact that it's noted by our people means it wasn't a couple of random conscripts nipping in for -- to answer a call of nature. It was a number of vehicles containing a number of relatively senior officers turning up with their briefcases and going in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The document doesn't have a date, but it does refer to an operation in Junik two days ago, on the 13th of December. Can we conclude from that the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I -- yes, I mean, I think -- therefore I suspect it was the 15th because one of the few sets of information we did have with us at the time was a calendar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I see that in the second bullet point in bold it is noted: "We are unable to verify without access to these areas." Can you please comment on that sentence that's been included in bold?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We were already starting to find that when we went somewhere we would be stopped by a check-point on the road who would say it's not safe enough for you to continue, you shouldn't go any further. And we therefore tended at that stage to do what was indicated in order to avoid antagonising the people on the ground. So in the first instances when we got to those points, we would stop, make a note of it, and bring it up at the official level saying, Look, how can we verify things if you don't let us go anywhere? And oh, by the way, you do remember that we're supposed to have complete freedom of movement throughout the area. And so you are not -- you are not sticking to the terms of the deal, and you are doing yourself no good at all by allowing this to happen because it gives us the impression that something suspicious is happening on the other side of where we're being blocked. And initially we got to a point, we were stopped, we reported back, we'd protest -- we'd protested, we followed the niceties of it. As time went on, we started to try to work our way around it and would look for another way, a back road that would get us to where we wanted to go, but that was later. To start with we tried to do it properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 02546, and ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like now to refer to an incident in Podujevo that you refer to in your statement and this is starting at paragraph 95 of your statement. You refer to an incident that developed over a number of days. In paragraph 95 you refer to the date of the 18th of December, 1998, and a report of a VJ armoured unit leaving barracks and moving to an airfield south of Podujevo and some paragraphs down from that, 99, you refer to a column of VJ and MUP leaving Pristina on the 24th of December. Do you recall this incident, and if you could provide us further details as to how this incident developed in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, this follows on from the earlier discussions about training and the -- having been told that there was a requirement to conduct out-of-barracks training and myself having said, Okay, in that case we need the full details of it, who's doing what, where, with what, when. That was not responded to, and then on the 18th of December, as you see, a number of armoured vehicles left the barracks in the west of Pristina and moved about 10 miles north to an area which was a few hundred metres by a few hundred metres which was enclosed by a wire fence and which was designated as military property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yeah, and just going back to my reference to paragraph 99 we see that some days later after that deployment occurred there was a further deployment of a column of VJ and MUP leaving Pristina on the 24th, and in paragraph 100 you refer to having passed that column. And in it you say that you note that they were not travelling separate parts of -- the VJ and MUP were not travelling separate parts of the column but rather evenly mixed throughout the convoy. Why was that significant?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: If you're putting together a column of a platoon of this comprising five vehicles, and a platoon from somewhere else comprising five vehicles, and a platoon from somewhere else comprising five vehicles, just the way that goes together tends to be A followed by B followed by C. And so if you suddenly find that the MUP are spread throughout the column, it indicates that this isn't a unit that has joined -- has just joined the group; it indicates that it's a series of police detachments, each of which is closely affiliated to one of the -- one of the subunits of the VJ. And so, my impression was that that was unusual, simply because if these groups had been told to come together at a certain place at a certain day and then go on up and do something, then you would have expected there to be six MUP vehicles nose to tail together, not spread throughout. So one of the reasons you might do that is so that the army has got a MUP vehicle with it so that the army and the MUP can communicate together on -- in an operation where both have a part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would now ask you to turn to the next tab.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 02537, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Tab 10?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Tab 10, yes. And this is a report which starts on the top with the heading: "Developments in the mission area." Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if you could comment on letter (a), paragraph 1(a).

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: As a result of the large number of vehicles going from barracks and from the -- from the location near Podujevo which we called the airfield, they went up to Podujevo, they went west of Podujevo, and they engaged KLA whom they found there whom they were aware of them, which was the purpose of their going there. And there was a considerable exchange of fire. The VJ and the MUP came up onto the hill and shelled positions where there was some KLA. So that describes the situation. I personally went up there and can testify that tank main armament was being fired, mortars were being fired because they have distinctive -- distinctive sounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at paragraph 102 you refer to a telephone conversation -- call from Colonel Mijatovic, who was reporting on that day, Nothing is going on. And you say this undermined his credibility as a MUP offensive from the village of Gornja Lapastica was going on at the time. Is this a different offensive than the one that is described in this document?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, it's the same general area. Gornja Lapastica is north-west of Podujevo, about 3 or 4 kilometres. So it's all describing the action that was going on west of Podujevo on a ridge about 2 kilometres -- it started about 2 kilometres west of Podujevo from Gornja Lapastica in the north to an area about 4 kilometres to the south. So it's an area about 4 kilometres by 2 or 3, about 12 square kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when I began asking you questions about the incident in Podujevo you referred back to an earlier answer you had given on training. How does training exercise relate to the action that was going on? Why did that come to mind?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The training that was said to be required was tank driver training, and the route that was described to me by General Loncar, showing me on the map, literally indicating with his finger on the map, showed me that they were going to go in a large circle broadly around Podujevo. And this was going to take them to the west of Podujevo, into this area that subsequently became a battle-ground. We were area, we were all aware, that the KLA were becoming active in this area and there had been sightings of the KLA and there had been the occasional -- occasional shot fired from the KLA in the general direction of -- of the road between Pristina and Podujevo. This was of concern to General Loncar because this was the main road between Pristina and Nis, in other words, the life-line to the rest of Serbia. The positions west of the road included some which had been occupied by the VJ during September and October and which had been vacated by the VJ by the Yugoslav side as a result of this. And their argument was reasonable that we should do our best to get these people off the hills and get them to go away, and we agreed. And we went and talked to them. I personally did so on at least one occasion and said, You are crazy doing this. You know that you will aggravate things on the ground and things will get worse and people will come after you. You need to go away. And they said, Thank you for your advice, and we'll think about it. At this stage there were two factors that needed to be remembered. One was that we were finding it very difficult to make a proper connection with the leadership of the KLA. We didn't really establish proper connection with the KLA until about a week later than this. So we were dealing with people as we bumped into them. That's the first thing. Second thing was that we weren't formally on the ground in this area because of the rate at which people were arriving and the need to go through a formal contracting procedure as we took over every location for our people. And the fact that it was being made very, very hard for us to do that by the Yugoslav authorities, we were only able to set up our regional centres, of which there were to be five, one at a time. And at this stage we broadly were covering with the 300 or so people we had the area to -- in the west of the country, the left-hand side of the country, and this did not include the Podujevo area. Now, we did this because the area that had seen the most violence in the summer was the area in the west and you have to start somewhere. I would much have preferred to have put people down all across the country, but I was not able to do that because I simply didn't have the ability to contract locations and set them up with communications and vehicles and IT in five different places simultaneously. That is certainly a matter of regret to me. When the first intimation happened that things were starting to hot-up in Podujevo, General Loncar requested me to increase the presence of the KVM there, in other words, to get somebody on the ground and we did that. And I got about a dozen people on the ground in advance of actually being able to have a proper centre to which they were reporting. So we did respond, but we could have -- it would have been nice to have responded more quickly. But I was -- this was a very blunt instrument we were putting together. It was not a well-honed set of units that had trained together, that had all their equipment, that had good procedures. This was an ad hoc latch-up, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, just going back to the start of your answer you referred to the fact that you had been notified that training was required for tank driving in this area. Based on what you were able to observe yourself and the reports that you received of what was going on, did what happened in this area between Podujevo and Gornja Lapastica result -- or, actually, was it really a training exercise that was happening in this area?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I went off on a tangent. When General Loncar indicated where the tanks would be exercising, I then discussed with him the fact that if they went into the areas that he had indicated, west of Podujevo, they would be quite likely to bump into these random KLA that were beginning to pop up. And I said that if the object of your exercise is to teach people driver training, then if you were to do that driver training east of Podujevo instead of west of Podujevo you would save yourself a lot of trouble because you would not bump into -- you would not run the risk of bumping into the KLA. And given the people that you're trying to train are people who not are not yet fully trained, it would be in my view a kindness to the people you're trying to train to not put them into that situation. His response was that, We will train where the heck we want to, and if we bump into any trouble, then we will take appropriate action. And I commented that if you go around that way you will certainly bump into trouble and you will know that you've bumped into trouble because you will have set out in order to bump into trouble. And he said, Well, we'll do what we are required to do. So that was a fairly uncompromising exchange, but that was what happened. And then, of course, they did go on their driver training exercise as indicated. They did drive west of Podujevo. They did get shot at. They did respond with tank main armament. They returned to their position to the south-east of Podujevo and this was probably the trigger for the subsequent operation that took place on the 24th of December, when the armoured column came out of Pristina and stormed the hills to the west of Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, the report we were just looking at, which is dated 24th December, speaks about both tank and mortar rounds were fired in addition to small arms fire in a confrontation with the UCK. We were talking earlier about proportionality and what you understood proportionality to mean. Based on what you were able to observe on the ground of how this operation in this general area of Podujevo was carried out, would you say that the response from both the MUP and the VJ to the KLA fire was proportionate?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It's quite a difficult one. It is at the very top end of what's proportionate. My first objection to what was going on was that no notice was given to us of what was proposed, and therefore we had no opportunity to discuss what their modus operandi was to be. If people are firing at you, you cannot -- you cannot simply totally ignore it, and therefore I think the use, for instance, of mortars onto an area and of -- the -- I would say if you used mortars and if you used tank machine-guns, that would be fine; if you use the occasional tank main armament round, that could be seen as justified. But the purpose of tank main armament is to destroy other tanks. It's generally not a very good area weapon, so it's not really the right weapon for the job. And the problem with a tank round is that when you fire a tank round it keeps going. It goes for miles and miles and miles, and so you've got no idea what it's going to hit at the other end. It could have been landed in Pristina for all we knew. So it wasn't really -- a tank main armament is not really the appropriate weapon used in large numbers, and we were aware of more than than the occasional tank main armament going off. So to repeat, I think it was at the high end of what was proportionate. But when you're dealing with conscripts, conscripts aren't trained very well and conscripts may have -- in order to keep conscripts moving, you may need to give them the psychological reassurance of a lot of -- a lot of things being fired towards the enemy. So that's another factor that has to be taken account of. So I don't think it was totally disproportionate at this stage, but it was not -- it could have been done better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit 02537, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1004, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, General, if we could now move to tab 11 of your binder, and this is 65 ter 02544. And we see that this is a document dated 25th December 1998, entitled main points of the meeting between General Lukic and DHOMOPS, and you are indicated as one of the persons being present. I'm interested in paragraph 2 of this document -- just if you could tell us if you are familiar with the document and if you could comment specifically on paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, Malisevo is quite far into the west of Kosovo. It is south-east of Pec. And it had been an area where there had been a lot of violence in the summer. The village is predominantly Kosovar Albanian, and it had a police station in the village. The police station was -- had been reinforced with sandbags and things so it looked really like a fort. The -- and the police that were in this police station were hunkered down in the police station and tended to stay in the police station. The only patrols they did were in armoured vehicles. Their presence was not like normal police. We felt that they were not making the place any more secure by their actions or their presence, and therefore we believed that we could help the situation by putting a permanent presence of our verifiers into the village. This particular place had some symbolism because early in December there had been a march of Kosovar Albanians to this area which had come very close to resulting in violence, and the situation had been talked down by the presence of two of my verifiers. So this was known to us. It was a bit of a co-celebre. So since then we had said, Look, we know the situation is unsustainable in Malisevo. We know that your policemen are unable to police the area properly. The local inhabitants feel thoroughly over-awed by what's going on. We are prepared to help by putting people in there, but you need to help us as well by making your presence there look less threatening to the locals. And that was the gist of the conversations that had gone on throughout December, and this was a follow-up meeting in regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 6, operations around Podujevo, these main points record you as stating that: "The ongoing VJ/MUP operation was a serious breach of the cease-fire and that any casualties sustained would be attributed directly to the FRY government." Could you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This was -- as the operation around Podujevo was starting to happen, and I was specifically referring to the fact that the VJ had chosen to do their training west of Podujevo which in my view had triggered this whole series of events, and therefore this was not a case of them saying, We have decided to do something about this area for the following reasons, that they had deliberately put themselves into a position against advice and having gone looking for trouble, trouble had found them, and they were escalating the situation to an unnecessary degree. And so that was the background to it, and of course as the 24th of December went on, we've seen that the -- everybody piled in to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that this is a meeting with General Lukic. Was this the first time that you had met with General Lukic?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at the time what did you understand General Lukic's role in Kosovo to be?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I understood him to be in command of the MUP in Kosovo, as it says at the top: "Present: General Lukic, commander of the Kosovo MUP."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe you also referred to this meeting in your statement at paragraph 103, just stating that for reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. This is 65 ter 02544, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1004, Your Honours -- I apologise, 1005.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, and just going back briefly to the situation in Podujevo, in paragraph 111 of your statement, last sentence, you say that: "It was extremely unlikely that the MUP commander in Podujevo would have acted independently without the VJ at least being informed."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry, give me the paragraph again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: 111. I'm referring to the last sentence which refers to a comment you're making, if you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This referred to a meeting at which -- between General Loncar and head of mission, Walker. The situation in Podujevo was a sort of armed standoff, and part of the immediate issue was the fate of, I think, an elderly Serb who had -- who had been killed. And the concern was to recover his body. And the issue was how to do that without re-igniting the exchanges of fire and getting more people killed and injured. And so I started off having a meeting with Loncar, which developed into a meeting with Walker; and at this we were trying to work out who should go, how many vehicles, what the escort should be, and so on. And we had our people with each side with radio vehicles, so we were in position to talk to both sides in this. And we were going through this. And at that point we were told that a MUP -- a series of MUP vehicles had gone to where the dead -- the body was and had attempted to get the body and a fire-fight had started. And my point is that in order to do this, the MUP vehicles had to leave the area where the MUP and VJ forces were and go forward into the area where it was quite likely that the KLA were. It was not -- it was not the specific area where we knew them to be, but we were -- we knew this was in the no man's land between the two and that was why we were keen that this was done sensitively so that we went and brought one body out and we didn't go in to bring one body out and end up bringing six bodies out because of casualties that took place. So we were trying to work out what was the best way of doing it was, and who would talk to whom, and how we would choreograph this operation in order to keep it as low-key as possible. And we got the message that while we were doing this discussion - and we understood that everybody had agreed that no one was going to move until we'd finished the discussion and come to some conclusions - that the MUP had apparently gone it alone. And my point at the bottom of the paragraph is that I simply don't believe that in a situation like that where people are manning heavy weapons with their fingers on the trigger thinking themselves the front line that the MUP would simply have driven out. You are in a situation where you are driving forward of tanks and heavy machine-guns manned by your own side, but by the army and you're the police. Now, would you do that on your own without coordinating with the army? Absolutely not. It's simply not credible. That is -- that's the point, that this must have been fixed in advance with the army units. Loncar was the -- our link to the army units, and Loncar was saying to us that he was completely unaware of this going on. And it was because of that that he forfeited the trust of Walker. And I don't think Walker ever spoke to him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Since we're on that page of the statement I would direct your attention to paragraph 117 which now refers to events in January 1999. And it states: "We started to receive reports about roadblocks being set up by vigilante Serb civilians south of Pristina ..." and there's a reference to both Pristina and Kosovo Polje municipalities. Was this the first instant that this occurred, that you saw civilians setting up roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was the first incident that I personally witnessed, and it was quite widespread in that we got reports that roadblocks set up by Serbs in Serb villages by civilians wearing ski masks and heavily armed with long-barrelled weapons were setting up this roadblock and stopping any movement of anybody. This effectively cut us in Pristina off from the south of Kosovo. And I personal went to the area of Kosovo Polje in order to see it, and I saw these individuals in civilian clothes with weapons who were stopping everybody and turning people away, and they indeed turned us away. What was remarkable in this was that unlike every other day of the year, there was no police to be seen. Now, it was quite unusual to drive for 500 yards anywhere in Kosovo and not go past a policeman, and yet here we were in broad daylight, a situation which went on for a number of hours, and the police appeared to be unaware of it and take no action at all on it. So the police were absolutely not doing their job of ensuring law and order in this area on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that you personally went to Kosovo Polje and observed this. Were you able to obtain any information as to how these civilians had obtained the weapons that they used that day?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Not directly, no. They were in -- a lot of them were in black Golf vehicles, and I was informed but was never able to check it that there were a mixture of people who had come in from outside Kosovo and locals who were making this point, which was to -- in my view, the point of the demonstration was to intimidate the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was this the only -- the only instance where you saw armed Serb civilians or were there other instances?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There were other instances where armed civilians were seen, notably at Racak. I didn't personally see them in that amount of detail there, but they were reliably reported to me by people whose judgement I trusted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said that you had been informed that these people you saw at this check-point at Kosovo Polje came from outside. Who provided that information to you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It may well have been one of our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I asked you about other instances other than Racak, were there instances where armed Serb civilians were seen by your verifiers?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I'm sure there were, but the ones that I can instantly call to memory were Racak and this incident in early January.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you to turn tab 12 of your binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 00664, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The document is now up on the screen. We see, General, that this is a document entitled Kosovo Verification Mission report for the period of 13 January 1999. We have spoken very briefly about the reporting that was carried out by your verifiers. Could you explain to us what sort of reporting was done and specifically in relation to this document if you could tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is a copy of the sort of -- well, of the report -- one of the reports that we sent daily up to -- up to Vienna. The way it was compiled was that at any moment we had a series of outstations, 40 something, throughout Kosovo. We hadn't got everyone on the ground on 13th of January, but we were putting down outstations throughout Kosovo so that there was an outstation which acted as a base for verifiers to live in that area and patrol around it and to get to know the situation around it. And they reported immediately if something happened that was dramatic, and if they didn't come across anything dramatic then they would make a report at the end of the day. These reports went from the coordination centres to the regional centres. Each regional centre was in charge of about eight of these coordination centres throughout its area, and then the regional centres reported up to Pristina to the head -- to the mission headquarters there. In the mission headquarters, there were a number of agencies which looked at all this stuff, took the necessary action to inform other people that might be involved in the immediate action, and began to put together a report of what had happened in the previous 24 hours and what it meant and what it might portend for the future. And so this was the -- and that -- the drafting of that report that went up to Vienna was something which was entrusted to a group of about three people who were the same people, so that there was a high level of consistency. Obviously, if they got some piece of information, they weren't sure about it, then they could go back to the author of the information and ask some more details. So this was the report that the head of mission signed off and sent up to Vienna, either last thing at night or first thing in the morning, which said what had happened in the last 24 hours of significance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We see in "General Situation" there's a sentence saying: "The fighting continues in Decani area with confirmed VJ involvement." I would ask you to turn the page to page 2, under the heading "Security Situation," and in the B/C/S copy this is on page 3. And I'm interested in the first paragraph that begins with: "The police operation in Gornji Ratis east of Decani continues for a fourth day ..." And I'm particularly interested in the last sentence of that paragraph, if you could comment on that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The point here is that this was described to us as a police action. This is a continuation of our increasingly being convinced that this was actually the police and the army acting entirely in concert. So it's a police action, but we confirmed the involved of the VJ in the second paragraph. We mention tank fire, and again heard the fire between 50 to 60 rounds, I mean, that's every round in the turret, that's a lot of large bullets being fired, and then the tank being sent away. And the point at the bottom for the benefit of the people in Vienna who of course are not dealing with this minute by minute that tanks have never been declared by the FRY authorities to be part of the police arsenal, and that reflected our understanding elsewhere that tanks were army equipment, they were not police equipment. And therefore, that was more evidence to us that these were combined operations, not police operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 00664, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be received as Exhibit P1006, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, just a moment ago you referred to the Racak incident. Is this incident described in some length in your statement, so I don't want to go through it in detail. I am interested, though, in a comment that is made in your statement and this is at paragraph 141 which is a paragraph starting with the sentence: "On Friday, the 15th of January, 1999 ..." And talks about a joint VJ/MUP offensive in the village of Racak. And the last sentence says: "It was a highly coordinated VJ and MUP operation ..." And I would like to ask you to explain why you made that statement in your statement.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There are two elements of this force were VJ that were sitting on high ground overlooking Racak about a kilometre away from Racak and the MUP who eventually went in to Racak. As this operation unfolded, there was a considerable amount of firing into the village, and then the firing switched from the village to the flanks of the village. And while firing was still going on, the MUP went into the village. Now, if you are walking forward of heavy weapons that are firing, then you need a pretty strong assurance that they know where they're firing and that they're not going to fire where you're going to go. This is not the sort of coordination you do casually. You would be very specific in saying that the tanks will now switch their fire so that they fire at nothing to the right of a certain point, and you will be going into an area on the other side of that point. So the tanks may be switching their fire so that they're going to fire at the flag and everything to the left of the flag, and we're going to go to the door. And then the other tanks will fire into the corner here and everything to the right of it. Now, if you've wired that really tight, if you've really coordinated that properly and it's being run by two people, one from the police and one from the army sitting side by side in the same location, then I would be prepared to go in -- go through that door under those circumstances. But remember that before then they'd been generally firing in the whole area, including at the door. And so at the moment that that fire switches, so the same amount of noise is going on but you know that they're not firing right at the flag and you know they're not firing left of the corner and you're going to go forward, that does require a very, very high degree of control. And the fact that it took place means that this was not an operation that was being done on a making-it-up-as-you-go-along basis, it must have been planned and there must have been a joint post controlling it. You simply wouldn't do it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you in relation to this incident to turn to tab 13 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 02547. If we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a document dated 5th January, and it says at the top: "Call to Colonel Kotur by MG DZ."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is a transcript of a phone call I made with an interpreter to Colonel Kotur. General Loncar was not available, and so I spoke to Colonel Kotur who was his assistant in these areas and who came to the periodic meetings with General Loncar generally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm interested in a statement that's made by you at the middle of the page which begins with: "Firing anti-aircraft weapons into villages with women and children is not a police action. This is not a police action."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is because we had observed during the day, and this was the Friday, it was the day that the Racak incident took place, and one of the weapons held by the VJ was a thing called the Praga anti-aircraft gun. And therefore it was a heavy anti-aircraft gun which obviously fired very large rounds very fast, and its normal role was to shoot down aircraft. And it had been observed firing into the village. And my point there was that this is not how you carry out police action, to fire indiscriminately into a village with a weapon which may go where you are aiming it but will keep going and go through the next six walls that it comes to; and if anybody happens to be in the way, it will slay them as well. And that is my point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I ask for this to be received. This is 65 ter 02547.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1007, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, it's again time for the break unless we're going to go a bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- because we started a bit late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I get the message. We will have a break, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I will continue. I will just write down the time we started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, we'll break now and resume hopefully on time at 1.00 and then finish the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In the interests of gaining time, Your Honour, I would ask to have exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, I cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you addressing us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes. I was just saying that in the interest of gaining time while the witness is being brought in, I would just like to ask for an exhibit to be put up in e-court. This is 65 ter 00673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, we're going to change topic now. We were just talking about the Racak incident. I want to direct your attention now to tab 14 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is for reference 65 ter 0073 [sic] which is already up on the screen. This is a KVM regional centre Prizren daily report, and it's dated 29th January 1999, and I want to direct your attention specifically to the section called: "Head of regional centre Prizren comments." If you could take a minute to look at that and provide your comments regarding that passage there.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is a comment from Mike Maisonneuve describing the incident at Rogovo the day before when a compound which we later found out to be a KLA safe house was stormed by a MUP special police unit and one of the special police was killed and 24 Albanians were killed. I personally attended this in the second half of the day some hours after the incident had happened and had a meeting with General Loncar at the time at the same place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that the comments that are included here by General Maisonneuve say: "The amount of force employed was not proportional. Not all persons were KLA. There is little evidence of fighting back as there is also little evidence of a large number of weapons." You've told us that you yourself went to the site. Were your conclusions on this incident consistent with what General Maisonneuve has stated here?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. It was my view that what had happened was that the compound was stormed by the special police unit in the early hours of the morning, and after an -- after the initial storming in which one of the MUP was killed and a number of the -- a number of the Albanians were killed, that the rest of them surrendered and were then killed by the MUP. Had that not been the case, then there would have been prisoners, there would have been wounded. It is almost impossible to kill 24 people and wound nobody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see that under the heading "Verification Tasks," that is on the same page at the bottom. It says: "Rogovo. "The VJ informed OSCE that they performed a supporting role only in the MUP operation, described below." Is this also consistent with the information you were able to obtain while on site?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is correct. On the actual site at a farm-house in Rogovo there were no VJ noted. They appeared to have provided an outer cordon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your statement - and this is at page 180 -- at paragraph 180, I'm sorry - the first line of that paragraph says: "The first time that I realised that the chains of command were much more closely linked than we thought was at the incident of Rogovo." Is this the same incident that this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why is it that you say that you realised that the chains of command were much more closely linked than you thought?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because General Loncar was there and was clearly in charge of what was a police operation or a police-led operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say "General Loncar was there," where exactly are you talking about, in the --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I'm talking about being inside the -- inside the compound and coming out of the compound when it was reported to him that I arrived, and then accompanying me into the compound when it was decided that I could go in. So he was on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: He was already on the scene when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 3. And I just very briefly want to have your comments on letter B which is entitled: "MUP and other police forces." And there's a report that we're not going to go through in detail because the document speaks for itself about the investigations that were carried out and the findings made by the KVM patrols. Which force -- you've told us about seeing General Loncar there. Which forces did you see on the ground when you got to Rogovo?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: When I got to Rogovo I was directed to a farm compound which had a wall 3 or 4 metres high and a closed gate which prevented me having access to it. So I stopped there, was met by one of my verifiers who told me what he knew, that there had been this incident, that the MUP and the dead Albanians were all inside the compound that I was not allowed to go into at that stage. While this was going on, there were a number of very fit-looking MUP coming out of the compound wearing grey all-in-one overalls which was different to anything I'd seen before. And in the court then-General Loncar appeared. We had a conversation. In the course of the conversation he showed me the body of one of these men in that same uniform in the back of a car, which appeared to indicate that that was the uniform in which -- which he'd been wearing when he was killed. These were not uniforms I ever saw again, and I got the firm impression that this was a Special Anti-Terrorist Unit that had been brought in specifically to do this operation. While I was in the area, the guys in the grey overalls faded out of the area; they basically packed up and left. And when I got into the compound there were none of them there. They -- the police in the compound were in the more traditional blue police camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It's 00673, and I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1008, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, just going back to your statement, paragraph 187, this is at the bottom of page 26 in the English, you refer to the period of February 1999 and you use an expression there that I would like to have your comments on which is - and this is in the middle of the paragraph - you refer to the cumulative effect of these feet on the ground. Could you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: What I mean is that there were a number of operations that were conducted in this time, and every time an operation was conducted in order to deal with KLA in a particular area if the Yugoslav forces were successful in taking that area then however many people had been involved in taking that area most of them would be withdrawn but a small garrison of 30 to 40 people would be left holding that particular position. And over the weeks, we observed these positions and we kept a running tally because obviously these were people who were not just leaving the barracks, going and doing something, and going back to barracks at the end of the day, these were people who were permanently out of barracks. And there came a moment when we were doing a routine report and counted them all up and said, Well, that amounts to about 2.000 people. And if you believe that a company is between 120 and 150 people then that's about 15 companies' worth. You could argue it was anything between 13 and 17, but it certainly was well in excess of three which was, of course, the only base-line that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we turn the page to paragraph 188 you talk about the period of March, 16 March, and you speak about the KVM becoming aware of the FRY declaring extending periods for conscripts and also an increase in the number of VJ personnel, and you refer also to the introduction of T-72 tanks by rail. Why is that significant? Why have you referred to the introduction of these type of tanks by rail in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because in the original very limited exchange of information that we had back in late November and December, the only tanks that were declared as being permanently stationed in Kosovo were the T-55 variety, which is obviously a different tank with a different crew and different -- different capabilities. And therefore, when we spotted T-72s being unloaded from rail flats near Mitrovica, it was clear that they had come in from outside. And therefore, while it was difficult to track people, it was not difficult to say, Look, here are T-72s, there aren't supposed to be any T-72s here, here they are, this is a breach.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: On that same page, and this is paragraph 190, you refer to two larger operations in the period late February/mid-March which occurred in the municipalities of Kacanik and Vucitrn. And you indicate, this is the third sentence, that the VJ and MUP were definitely on the offensive at this stage and will seal off areas where they were conducting operations, denying entry to the KVM. Could you please comment on that statement you make there in relation to these two operations.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, we would -- we -- by this stage we had people stationed on the ground throughout Kosovo, and so wherever something happened, we had someone on hand to see it begin to happen. And when operations happened in these areas, the first thing we would know about it would be when a convoy of military or police went by, there would then be an attempt to follow it and track it to see where it was going and what it was doing, and at some point we would get -- my verifiers would get to a point where there was a roadblock on the road, a sentry who would say, I'm sorry, you can't go any further. And at this point we would say, Well, we need to go further, because we have to see what's going on; we have freedom of movement. And he would say, Yes, but I'm afraid you can't go any further because we can't guarantee your safety if you go any further. This would then be reported up the line to us in Pristina, and we would then have to work out what to do. Sometimes I would send a more experienced team out because not everybody was equally experienced. Sometimes I would go myself. In the case of the incident described at paragraph 190, that describes a moment when I went myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in that paragraph you refer to company-sized units of the MUP - this is toward the middle of the paragraph - fitter-looking personnel and -- which were noticeably higher than other MUP units you had encountered to date. Was this also an observation you made yourself, of these company-sized MUP units?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the area for several hours, but towards the end of the afternoon - and this was an area where I had also got to a point where I had been stopped - the area beyond where I had been stopped where the operation appeared to be being carried out was characterised by plumes of smoke from burning buildings and round about 4.00 to 5.00 the -- this group of a hundred or more MUP appeared moving in a disciplined way, uniformed differently to the regular MUP we met because the regular MUP had blue uniforms. These guys were wearing green camouflage uniforms. Their webbing equipment was a more recent pattern, a better pattern. Their -- the sort of equipment they were carrying was different to that which most of the MUP normally carried. So this looked like a unit that was better trained, better equipped, and probably was deployed specifically to this area, as opposed to being indigenous to this area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you able to obtain any information as to when this unit had been deployed to this area?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, I mean we saw it for the first time that day, and we had seen other units similar to it in the south of the country, but I cannot say whether it was the same unit or it was just two units that were similarly equipped, but there were not many units so equipped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you to turn to tab 15 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 05335, if we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a document that is addressed to you from the head of RC 2, a Mr. Windmar, and the subject is protest against VJ and MUP.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: As you can see, at some stage I have written in my handwriting on this that this document is thought to have originated on or about the 12th of March, i.e., about a week before we were ordered out of Kosovo. This is from the head of Regional Centre 2, Leif Windmar, who was situated in Mitrovica, and he was responsible for the area particularly to the south and west of Mitrovica where there was a range of hills that -- that ran north-west to south-east parallel to the main road from Mitrovica down to Pristina. And the situation that he describes is the situation that we then paid more attention to, and I think it was as a result of this that I concentrated on the area and ended up with the entry in the earlier document that you saw. My problem in all of these instances was that when I took these complaints to the various liaison officers, I would invariably be told that I needed to provide specific times, dates, and identifications of everybody involved so -- because without that it was impossible to know whether or not we were hallucinating. And so this probably triggered my putting extra resources into the area and eventually led to me being there in the manner I've described.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is again a reference to the earlier operation you referred to in the Vucitrn area?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is a reference to operations in the Vucitrn area that at the time I was not fully -- fully aware of that led to me putting more experienced people on the ground there and led to me eventually being there and seeing for my own eyes the better-equipped, differently dressed MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We would like to direct your attention to paragraph 5 of this document which starts with: "VJ/MUP are now coordinating their activities in a much better way than before and it is ... obvious that they are performing a planned operation against the Albanian population and not like before, single response to KLA attacks or winter exercises." Could you comment on that passage here in this report.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The point there was that the areas were not simply being visited and left, but that there appeared to be a systematic drive that had cordoned off an area and then the VJ and the MUP were operating inside it systematically to completely clear the area of KLA. And by implication, displacing the Albanian population who happened to live there who obviously were suspected of giving assistance to the -- to the KLA or possible being KLA by night and farmers by day, which was quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in this same document - and this is paragraph 3 - refers to: "The behaviour of the VJ/MUP is also encouraging the civilian Serb population to participate in operations against civilian Albanians and against us." Could you provide more information as to what exactly was happening that led to this comment in the report.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think that's all I have on this particular piece because I cannot remember getting specific chapter and verse that armed civilians were doing anything at a particular place at a particular time, but this officer in charge of Regional Centre 2 was a very experienced person who had been in post for a large number of weeks by then. And so if Windmar told me something, I had no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: There is also a reference at the bottom of -- at the almost-to-last paragraph to the presence of paramilitary units from Serbia. I don't know if you see that.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This may have been the guys in the green camouflage uniforms, but I don't know. Again, this was something which we said, Right, how much do you know about it? Give us as much evidence as you can. We were getting no clues as to what was happening from our liaison meetings with the MUP and we'd rather given up, frankly, on expecting reports that these sort of things were happening. But if the situation in a particular area had been such that after a lot of consideration the decision by the Serb authorities was that a unit would come in from Serbia, would carry out an operation, and then return, the way to have legitimatised this would have been to have informed us in advance and this never happened. And so we saw these things but there was never any attempt to tell us in advance or, indeed, to tell us after the event. And all the attempts to find out from the Serb side, what they were doing in this area, were met with rebuttals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So I take it from your answer that what is being reported here in Leif Windmar's report was actually communicated up to the liaison officials from both the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it was yet another area where we said we know or we strongly suspect that units from Serbia are coming into Kosovo. If this is the case, you have to tell us. And it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this into evidence. It is 65 ter 05335, and ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1009, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to turn now to the next tab, 16, in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 02533 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a handwritten document dated Wednesday, 17th March, 1999. I'm interested in -- well, if you first could explain what this document is and I'm particularly interested in the sentence in the middle of the page which says "distinct change of Belgrade attitude ..." and there are two colons.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, there is another page taken from one of my notebooks, and as you can see it is a note of what -- the discussions that took place and the instructions that were given at the 8.00 meeting on Wednesday, the 17th of March. At 8.00 the head of the mission routinely met with the deputy heads of mission and a few others to review the previous day, work out what needed to be done today, and to give the head of mission advance notice of the sort of thrust that was to be briefed to him in the more formal 9.00 meeting where all the heads of department would present their -- their reports to him. The 8.00 meeting was very much an attempt to make sure that the head of mission and his deputies understood the questions that were likely to be posed to them at 9.00, the areas where guidance would be required, and an attempt to help the head of mission to -- to not be surprised by what he was going to be asked, to give him time to reflect, so that we could have a meeting at which guidance was given to the mission without an unseemly spat involving other deputy heads which had been known to happen. So this was trying to -- this was us trying to, what I would call, get the ducks in a row if that translates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And as I mentioned, I'm interested in the passage which says: "Distinct change of Belgrade attitude: "Not reinforcing by stealth. "Reinforcing overtly."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this consistent with what --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is my note, and I'm sure this is what I was saying to the head of mission, that everything we see indicates that Belgrade has changed its approach, that they have given up doing things and denying them, they are now doing things that are so obvious that it is impossible to avoid tripping over them. Reinforcing overtly and reinforcing by stealth referred to the T-55s versus the T-72s, the fact that there had been a public announcement that the conscripts who were due to be discharged next would not be discharged but would be retained and the next class of conscripts would be brought in which was obviously was going to increase the numbers substantially. And the third bullet the "change to the border zone" was again something which was published in the Official Gazette up in Belgrade which said that the border zone, a 5-kilometre zone around the border of Serbia which was known as the border security zone in which different rules applied because on which its proximity to the border particularly with Albania, that this zone was to be doubled overnight to 10 kilometres and that we weren't going to be allowed to operate inside this 10-kilometre zone. Now, this was significant because some of the major routes would have been affected by this doubling and several of our coordination centre locations were located inside the 10-kilometre zone. So we found it astonishing that this had been apparently decided which was a major change to the ability of the KVM to operate without any consultation, either with the OSCE in Vienna or with ourselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit. It is 02533. I ask that that be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1010.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could now turn to the next tab.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 02542.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I'll just give you a moment, General, to look at that document. It's a document which has your -- bears your name at the top and says "chief of operations, Kosovo Verification Mission."

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah, I recognise it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is the speaking notes that I used at a press conference in the UK Ministry of Defence when I was called back from Kosovo to my Ministry of Defence by my foreign minister to brief him first-hand on what was going on and how much we knew. We evacuated -- we drove out of Kosovo on the 20th of March with all of the internationals, and many of the interpreters and security people who were locals were left behind. And we left them their mobile phones with them. So once we had got into Macedonia, we continued to contact these people on the ground and to ask them what was going on, what was their impression of what was going on. And obviously this was the only way we could tell of what was going on because we weren't there. There were no internationals left. There was a lot of wild talk in the press at the time, and I was extremely keen that we did not add to the wild talk in the press by giving authenticity to reports that might well be thoroughly inaccurate and might well be put out simply to escalate the situation. So I told my people that we should get the best information we could and we should review it and we should only give credence to things that appeared to be supported from more than one source. Obviously if we'd been there we'd have gone up and seen whatever it was or we'd have talked in person to the -- face-to-face with the person we wanted to get this from, but this was the best we could do at the time. But in order to only say things which I felt were plausible and were supported by more than one person who was known to us, we carried out a very severe culling of the stories that were coming out of Kosovo. And so what I have here is the things that were absolutely as positive as we can be about them, and excluding a huge number of wild statements that came from people that we didn't know or were so wild as to be incredible. So this was the best we could do. And I have to say that I set about this because sitting in Macedonia I was being rung up by all sorts of people demanding atrocity stories saying, you must know that something really bad's going on, how much do you know about this or that? And I said, Look, we are trying to find this stuff out, and when we've got something we can tell you, we will do so. But we're not going to add to the speculation. Now, 12 days after coming out, I think we still had a reasonable grip on people we knew and they were generally in places that they were familiar with. And so we had a reasonable certainty that what we were describing certainly had happened. Other bad things may have happened but we weren't aware of them, but we believed that this was the absolute minimum that was happening and we were able to give some credibility to this. So we're not saying that this was all that was happening; we're saying this is definitely happening. Worse stuff may be happening, but we don't have credible reports of it at this stage. I then -- I spent the day from about 6.00 in the morning till that evening in London. This was part of a routine, daily Ministry of Defence press conference which was given every day during the Kosovo crisis, and I was brought on to make this statement in front of the media. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you help us. We see that the document is undated. Can you help us with the date when you believe this press conference was given?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, it was at the end of March/beginning of April because I say "as you know we were ordered out 12 days ago ..." we were ordered out on the 19th of March and we drove out on the 20th. So if we add 12 days to the 19th or the 20th, it's about the 32nd [sic] of March, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And can you tell us something about who all attended this conference that you gave where you gave this information and if this document was disseminated in any way?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was given in the main hall of the UK Ministry of Defence. The regular briefer who is a -- I think a two-star -- a major-general rank officer gave the introduction and then handed it over to me. The BBC was present as were the major news networks -- the other major news networks. I am pretty sure that a transcript was made available as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if you could very briefly turn to page 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is on page 1 of the B/C/S, page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see an account there it starts: "But the overall picture is bleak going around Kosovo starting in the north... " And there's a mention of different localities and events. Is this the information that you were telling us about that you had obtained --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- from sources on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which you later checked to verify before --

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, every one of these facts was given to us by at least two sources known to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now if we can go to the last page of the document, last paragraph, there is a paragraph starting by the word -- a sentence: "Finally, we must remember that the refugees we're seeing at the borders are the lucky ones, for they have escaped. We remain extremely concerned at the fate of those still in Kosovo, for many of them have been in the open for several days now." Can you comment on that passage of these speaking notes?

utterances.speaker: KAROL JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- the first thing is we were just starting to see refugees appearing at the border of Serbia and Macedonia, and they were appearing in fairly bad shape on foot, having been robbed along the way. And so -- and they were in -- there was several thousand, but we knew that there was several thousand of a total population in Kosovo of several million. And these were the people who had got out of Kosovo, and it was quite clear that if Podujevo and places like Malisevo were almost deserted, then the populations of these quite large towns had gone somewhere. They had gone somewhere and were in the hills somewhere. And this was quite early in the year. If everybody's on foot walking 60 miles through the hills, this is -- this is not a hike on a Sunday afternoon. This is -- this is a project where people -- a lot of people could end up dying because they're out in the open without food, without water, of exposure. So that was the point I was making.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the end of the session. I seek to tender this exhibit before we conclude today. This is 02542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I had to pre-empt the admission of this document. First of all, this is a typed document, not handwritten, and it's not dated. None of the sources cited in the document cannot be verified. The witness himself said that this had derived from some contacts with some people that they had used to work together on the ground before. Therefore, I don't think that this document fulfils the conditions required for admission. However, if this has been read at the briefing session in the UK or at the press conference, we would have had a report from the Whitehall on that which would say that a report was adopted in the Whitehall where the general took the floor and spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't need to hear from you, Ms. Kravetz. We will receive the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1011, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Principally, Mr. Djurdjic, because it is the witness's own document and he verifies its conduct. To the extent it reveals matters told to him rather than matters of his own knowledge, that is well explained in the evidence and we will consider it accordingly. We must now adjourn. We resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
